title: Review: Cell signaling and receptors (general); Hormones and the endocrine system; Control of gene expression: transcription factors and epigenetics
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for AP Biology (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: HO08b#t4 term and clue written for the game; HO02a#t3 term and clue written for the game; HO02a#t2 term and clue written for the game; HO08b#t1 term and clue written for the game. Questions: GR01a#N.6, HO02a#N.11, HO02b#N.11a, HO08b#N.11, GR01a#N.12, HO02a#N.3b, HO02b#N.7a, HO08b#N.6, GR01a#N.4a, HO08b#N.14, GR01a#N.2, GR01a#N.11. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Apoptosis
items.clue: Programmed cell death: a normal, controlled process, as between developing fingers.

items.label: Target cell
items.clue: It alone responds to a blood-borne signal, because it carries complementary receptors.

items.label: Hormone
items.clue: Signal secreted into the blood; slower to start but longer-lasting than a nerve impulse.

items.label: GPCR
items.clue: Receptor made of one chain crossing the membrane seven times; activates a relay on the inner face.

questions.stem: Oestrogen is a steroid hormone that passes through the plasma membrane of its target cells. How does oestrogen alter the pattern of gene expression in these cells?

options.text: It binds to a receptor protein, and the hormone–receptor complex acts as a transcription factor
It binds directly to the promoters of its target genes in place of a transcription factor
It activates enzymes already in the cell by binding to their active sites, without any transcription
It adds methyl tags to cytosine in the promoters of target genes, switching them on

questions.stem: In humans, cells of the pituitary gland at the base of the brain release human growth hormone, and target cells in many tissues respond, leading to growth. Which flowchart best represents how this signal reaches and affects its target cells?

options.text: Pituitary cell → blood → cells all over the body → every cell reached responds → growth
Pituitary cell → one vessel to target tissue alone → target cells respond → growth
Pituitary cell → nerve impulse down the spinal cord → target cells respond → growth
Pituitary cell → blood → cells all over the body → only cells with receptors respond → growth

questions.stem: Inside liver cells, the enzyme phosphodiesterase breaks cAMP down to an inactive product. Caffeine inhibits phosphodiesterase. Liver cells are given caffeine and then a low dose of adrenaline. Compared with cells given adrenaline alone, what is predicted?

options.text: No difference: adrenaline itself enters the cell and activates the glycogen-breaking enzymes, so cAMP does not matter.
More glucose released: the extra cAMP leaves the cell and stimulates neighbouring liver cells.
More glucose released: the extra cAMP itself breaks glycogen down into glucose.
More glucose released: cAMP is removed more slowly, so protein kinase stays active longer.

questions.stem: A mutation changes the intracellular domain of a G protein-coupled receptor so that it activates its G protein whether or not ligand is bound. The ligand-binding domain is unchanged. What is predicted?

options.text: No response at all, because a mutated receptor can no longer bind its ligand.
A response only when extra ligand is added, to make up for the mutation.
The pathway is active even with no ligand bound, so the response continues all the time.
No change, because only mutations in the ligand-binding domain affect signalling.

questions.explanation: The G protein is activated whether or not ligand is present, so everything downstream stays switched on.

questions.stem: In a skin cell, the promoter of gene G is methylated and the gene is not expressed. The cell divides by mitosis. What is the most likely state of gene G in the daughter cells, and why?

options.text: Not expressed, because the methyl tags remained in place through mitosis
Expressed, because epigenetic tags are lost whenever DNA is replicated
Not expressed, because the methylation has changed the base sequence of the gene
Not expressed in the person's children, because the tags pass to offspring

questions.explanation: Tags such as promoter methylation can remain in place during mitosis, so the daughter cells inherit the same pattern of gene expression. The base sequence of gene G is unchanged.

questions.stem: A hormone released into the blood by a gland affects only some of the body's cell types. Which statement best explains why only these cell types respond to it?

options.text: The gland sends the hormone straight to its target cells, so other cell types do not receive it.
The cell types that respond let the hormone in, and a hormone acts on a cell only from inside it.
The cell types that respond have receptors that recognize the hormone; other cell types lack them.
Cells close to the gland receive enough hormone to respond, but cells far away get too little.

questions.stem: A few epinephrine (adrenaline) molecules binding to receptors on a liver cell can lead to the release of millions of glucose molecules. Which statement best explains this amplification?

options.text: Each epinephrine molecule enters the cell and breaks down many glycogen molecules itself.
Each activated molecule in the cascade activates many of the next, so numbers multiply.
The cell makes extra copies of epinephrine inside, so more hormone acts on the glycogen.
Each phosphate added by a kinase supplies the energy to release one glucose molecule.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly describes the events after epinephrine (adrenaline) binds to its receptor on a liver cell?

options.text: Epinephrine enters the liver cell and directly activates the enzymes that break down glycogen into glucose.
cAMP is released from the liver cell into the blood as a second messenger that acts on other liver cells.
A G protein is activated, adenylyl cyclase converts ATP to cAMP, and cAMP activates kinases that switch on glycogen breakdown.
The activated G protein converts ATP into cAMP, and the cAMP then breaks glycogen down directly into glucose.

questions.explanation: The activated G protein switches on adenylyl cyclase, cAMP activates protein kinases, and the phosphorylated enzymes break down glycogen.

questions.stem: In a hypothetical species of yeast, protein P represses gene G by binding to a DNA sequence next to the promoter of gene G. A mutation changes this DNA sequence so that protein P can no longer bind to it. Which prediction about cells with this mutation is correct?

options.text: Protein G would have a different amino acid sequence, as gene G has mutated.
Gene G would be transcribed even with protein P present, as P no longer blocks it.
Gene G would no longer be transcribed, as protein P could not bind to switch it on.
The cells would make extra protein P so that it could still bind and repress gene G.

questions.stem: Drug Z inhibits phosphodiesterase, the enzyme that breaks down cAMP. Liver cells treated with Z are given a short pulse of epinephrine, which is then washed away. Compared with untreated cells, what is predicted?

options.text: Glycogen breakdown stops the moment epinephrine is washed away, so Z makes no difference.
No glycogen breakdown at all, because Z blocks the epinephrine receptor.
cAMP leaves the treated cells and activates glycogen breakdown in neighbouring cells.
cAMP stays high for longer, so glycogen breakdown continues for longer.

questions.explanation: The pathway is switched on as normal, but its off-switch is blocked. cAMP lingers, kinases stay active and glycogen breakdown is prolonged.

questions.stem: Developing red blood cells produce large amounts of the beta chain of haemoglobin, but liver cells produce none, although both cell types contain the gene. Which statement explains the difference?

options.text: Liver cells lost the gene when they differentiated, so they no longer contain the DNA sequence for the beta chain.
The gene is transcribed in developing red blood cells but not in liver cells, so liver cells make no mRNA for the protein.
Both cell types transcribe the gene, but only red blood cells translate the mRNA into the beta chain polypeptide.
Both cell types make the beta chain, but liver cells break the protein down as soon as it has been produced.

questions.stem: Cytosine bases in the DNA of a gene's promoter become methylated. What is the effect on the gene?

options.text: Translation of the gene's mRNA is blocked, because ribosomes cannot read methylated codons
The base sequence of the gene is altered, so a different polypeptide is produced from it
Transcription of the gene is increased, because the methyl tag marks it for expression
Transcription of the gene downstream is repressed, so it is not expressed

questions.explanation: Methylation of cytosine in a promoter represses transcription and therefore expression of the gene downstream, without any change in the base sequence.
